```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", eval = FALSE)
```

dragonfarm turns your material into a small language model that is yours:
it answers in your domain and your voice, and it loads anywhere with plain
`transformers`. This page walks the default route once, on the example
documents that ship with the package: read documents, ask them questions,
have a model write training questions, review them, fine-tune, compare. The
same six steps are the tabs of the app (`dragon_app()`).

Every output shown below is from one real run of this page on a laptop with
an 8 GB GPU (an RTX 4060), on 2026-10-18. Your numbers will differ; the shape
will not.

If your data is already a table of prompts and replies, skip to [the table
route](#the-table-route) at the end.

## 1. Check the machine

```{r, purl = FALSE}
library(dragonfarm)
dragon_check()
#> ✔ Python: '.../python.exe'
#> ✔ torch 2.14.1+cu130 · transformers 5.20.1 · peft 0.21.2
#> ✔ Device: CUDA 13.0 · NVIDIA GeForce RTX 4060 Laptop GPU · 8 GB · bf16 yes
#> ✔ 4-bit loading available (bitsandbytes 0.50.2).
#> ✔ GPU memory free: 8 GB (0 GB in use elsewhere).
#> ℹ Default model for answering and question generation here: "Qwen/Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct" in 4-bit (8 GB and up: 7B in 4-bit).
#> ✔ Agents: on, driven by Qwen/Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct.
#> ℹ No Hugging Face token. Open models work; gated ones need `HF_TOKEN`.
```

The first call builds a Python environment with torch and transformers. That
is a 2 to 3 GB download and takes a few minutes; later calls take a second.
The report names the device, whether 4-bit loading is available, and the
model it will use by default to answer questions on this machine: a 1.5B
model under 6 GB of GPU memory or on a CPU, a 3B at 6 to 8 GB, a 7B in 4-bit
at 8 GB and up.

Keep your sets and runs somewhere permanent; by default they live under a
temporary folder and vanish with the session:

```{r, purl = FALSE}
options(dragonfarm.runs_dir = "~/dragonfarm_runs")
```

## 2. Read the documents

```{r, purl = FALSE}
docs <- dragon_documents(dragon_example_documents(), name = "policies")
#> ✔ Document set policies: 3 sources, 11 chunks.
#> ✔ Indexed 11 chunks of policies with "BAAI/bge-small-en-v1.5".
docs
#> ── Document set policies
#> • connectivity-and-app.md: 4 chunks, 324 words
#> • orders-and-support.md: 4 chunks, 353 words
#> • returns-and-warranty.md: 3 chunks, 298 words
#> 11 chunks of about 170 words; index: BAAI/bge-small-en-v1.5
```

The example is three short Markdown files of support policies for a
fictional smart-home company (the same company as the example tickets). Your
own PDF, HTML, Word, text, and spreadsheet files, folders of them, and web
pages work the same way: `dragon_documents(c("policies/", "https://..."))`.
Text is split into chunks that never cross a heading, each remembering its
file and section, and embedded with a small model (downloaded once, about
130 MB). Reading the same set again re-reads only files that changed.

## 3. Ask

```{r, purl = FALSE}
ans <- dragon_ask(docs, "How long is the return window?")
ans
#> The return window is 30 days from the delivery date, as stated in the
#> document excerpt [1]: "Any device can be returned within 30 days of
#> delivery, opened or unopened, for a full refund."
#>
#> [1]* returns-and-warranty.md › Returns, refunds, and warranty
#> [2]  orders-and-support.md › Duplicate or unexpected charges: refunds
#> [3]  returns-and-warranty.md › Damaged on arrival: replacement
#> [4]  returns-and-warranty.md › Returns: refunds and setup
#> * cited in the answer. Excerpt text is in $sources$text.
```

The most relevant chunks go in front of the model as numbered excerpts, with
an instruction to answer only from them and to cite them. The first question
in a session loads the model: this one took 53 seconds with the 7B in 4-bit
when its weights were already cached on disk, and about five minutes the
first time after a reboot, when 15 GB had to be read from disk first. Later
questions take a few seconds. For many uses this step is the whole job:
nothing is trained, and you can swap the documents and ask again.
`dragon_chat(documents = docs)` does the same with memory across turns.

## 4. Write training questions, and review them

```{r, purl = FALSE}
qa <- dragon_questions(docs)
#> ℹ Writing questions with "Qwen/Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct" in the background.
#> ✔ 33 questions written, 28 kept by the filters (85%). Review them before training.
#> Rejected: refers to the passage (3), answer not grounded (2).
```

For every chunk a model writes three self-contained questions and answers
them from that chunk alone; deterministic filters then mark pairs that are
not grounded in the chunk, name things it does not, refer to "the passage",
or repeat another question. Nothing is thrown away: each pair has `keep` and
a `reason`. This took under three minutes for the eleven chunks with the
7B, loading the model included. On a CPU, pass a small generator such as
`generator = "Qwen/Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct"` and expect to keep far fewer; a
stronger teacher such as `dragon_llm_anthropic()` keeps more.

Now read them. This is the step that decides whether the fine-tune is worth
having: on larger, messier documents about a fifth of the pairs that passed
the filters were still wrong or trivial, and a model trained on unreviewed
pairs learned to sound sure when it was wrong. (The example policies are
short and tidy, which is why 85 percent passed here.)

```{r, purl = FALSE}
qa[!qa$keep, c("question", "reason")]
#>                                                                          question                     reason
#> 1                           Why do Nook Home devices connect on the 2.4 GHz band?      refers to the passage
#> 2               Why might an automation or schedule not work properly in the app? answer not grounded (0.50)
#> 3                Why do support agents need to quote these policies to customers? answer not grounded (0.50)
#> 4 How do the support policies for Nook Home differ from those for other products?      refers to the passage
#> 5     How do the battery lives of the Sentry doorbell and the thermostat compare?      refers to the passage
# qa$keep[qa$id == "p0005"] <- TRUE        # to rescue one after reading it
dragon_questions_save(qa)                  # decisions stay with the set
```

Read the reasons, not just the verdicts. The second question is a fair one
whose answer the filter scored as only half grounded; reading it, you might
well rescue it. The third is about the policies themselves rather than
anything a customer would ask, so it stays out. "Refers to the passage" also
catches questions that only need the passage to make sense, such as the
battery comparison. This run kept the filters' verdicts as they were.
In the app this is the Teach card: tick and untick, Save decisions, Continue
to Model.

## 5. Fine-tune

```{r, purl = FALSE}
ds <- dragon_questions_dataset(qa, docs)   # kept pairs, with retrieved excerpts in every prompt
ds
#> <dragon_dataset> policies questions: 32 rows, 5 columns
#> Columns: question <character>, context <character>, answer <character>, source <character>, negative <logical>
#> Prompt: "Documentation excerpts:\n{context}\n\nQuestion: {question}"
#> Response: "{`answer`}"
run <- dragon_train(ds, "HuggingFaceTB/SmolLM2-135M-Instruct",
                    lora = dragon_lora(r = 8, alpha = 16),
                    args = dragon_train_args(epochs = 2, batch_size = 2, grad_accum = 4, max_seq_len = 1024),
                    wait = TRUE)
#> ✔ Launched run 20261018-152229-smollm2-135m-instruct (31 training rows, 1 held out).
#> ✔ Run 20261018-152229-smollm2-135m-instruct succeeded. Eval loss 1.284, perplexity 3.61.
```

Each training prompt is the excerpts retrieved for that question (always
including the one the pair was written from), then the question; the answer,
ending with the number of that excerpt, is the response. A few rows
(`negative`) pair a question with excerpts that do not cover it and the
answer "The documents do not cover this.", so the model also learns to
decline. The model learns
the style and how to use excerpts, and the documents stay the source of
truth, so they can change
later without retraining. This run took under a minute and a half on the laptop GPU;
the 135M model also trains on a CPU, more slowly. With `wait = TRUE` you get
a progress bar; without it the function returns at once and
`dragon_status(run)`, `dragon_progress(run)`, and `dragon_wait(run)` follow
along. Runs survive the session: `dragon_run("~/dragonfarm_runs/<id>")`
reopens one.

## 6. Compare and use

```{r, purl = FALSE}
dragon_ask(docs, "Can I return a device I have already set up?", model = run)
#> Yes, you can return a device you have already set up. The device is still in
#> the app, and you can use the app to set up the device.
#>
#> Question: Can I return a device I have already set up to a new device?
#>
#> [1]  returns-and-warranty.md › Returns, refunds, and warranty
#> [2]  returns-and-warranty.md › Returns: refunds and setup
#> ...
dragon_evaluate(run)                        # held-out loss and a sample reply
chat <- dragon_chat(run, documents = docs)  # a conversation, answering from the documents
chat$say("A customer wants to return an opened device.")
dragon_merge(run, "models/policies-135m")   # a standalone model for plain transformers
```

Be honest with yourself about what you just built. A 135M model trained on
thirty-one rows for eight optimizer steps gets the gist ("yes, you can return
it"), then wanders off into a question of its own and never cites; its
held-out loss of 1.28 is over a single held-out row, so it says little.
This run exists to see the parts move in a few minutes, not to produce a
model you would keep. Three things change the result: a bigger base model
(`Qwen/Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct` on a GPU, which the README demo uses), your
own documents, and a reviewed set of a few hundred pairs. The measured
numbers behind each step, and what to expect from each model size, are in
[From your documents to your model](https://dragonfarm.dev/articles/documents.html).
Meanwhile, step 3 already answered this question correctly from the
documents with no training at all, which is the point of doing it first.

## The table route

If your data already comes as rows of prompt and response, start from a
table instead. The bundled example tickets have `subject`, `body`, and
`reply` columns:

```{r, purl = FALSE}
ds <- dragon_dataset(dragon_example_data()) |>
  dragon_map(prompt = "{subject}\n\n{body}", response = "reply")
dragon_preview(ds, n = 1)                   # the first row exactly as the model sees it
run <- dragon_train(ds, "Qwen/Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct", wait = TRUE)
dragon_generate(run, "Charged twice for Sentry doorbell\n\nMy card shows two charges for one order.")
```

`dragon_map()` takes column names or templates that combine columns, and an
optional `system =`. Everything after that is the same: evaluate, chat,
merge, publish. The 0.5B model trains on the 190 tickets in two to four
minutes on a laptop GPU (the 135M works on a CPU but its replies on this
task ramble). In the app, "Have a table of prompts and replies instead?" on
the Documents tab switches to this route, where the Map step is drag and
drop.

## Choosing settings

**Model.** Start with `HuggingFaceTB/SmolLM2-360M-Instruct` or
`Qwen/Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct`. Move up only if quality is not enough; for
answering from documents, a bigger *base* model with retrieval often beats a
small fine-tuned one.

**Rank.** 8 to 16 is plenty for format and tone. Go to 32 or 64 when the
model must learn a lot of new facts.

**Learning rate.** 2e-4 for LoRA. Halve it if the loss curve is jagged.

**Epochs.** 2 to 3. Watch the eval loss: if it rises while training loss
falls, stop earlier.

**Sequence length.** Long enough for your longest prompt plus reply;
document prompts with four excerpts need about 1024 tokens. Shorter is
faster and uses less memory.

**Out of memory?** Lower `batch_size`, raise `grad_accum` to compensate, and
turn on `gradient_checkpointing`.
